325	### Manual filtering: file types
326	
327	Over time, you might notice that you use the same glob patterns over and over.
328	For example, you might find yourself doing a lot of searches where you only
329	want to see results for Rust files:
330	
331	```
332	$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
333	```
334	
335	Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for
336	file types:
337	
338	```
339	$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
340	```
341	
342	or, more succinctly,
343	
344	```
345	$ rg 'fn run' -trust
346	```
347	
348	The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is
349	assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you
350	write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For
351	example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source
352	files and C header files:
353	
354	```
355	$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
356	```
357	
358	or you could just use the C file type:
359	
360	```
361	$ rg 'int main' -tc
362	```
363	
364	Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too:
365	
366	```
367	$ rg clap --type-not rust
368	```
369	
370	or, more succinctly,
371	
372	```
373	$ rg clap -Trust
374	```
375	
376	That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude
377	files of this type."
378	
379	To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`:
380	
381	```
382	$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
383	make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
384	```
385	
386	By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these
387	types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own
388	types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which
389	consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS:
390	
391	```
392	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
393	```
394	
395	or, more succinctly,
396	
397	```
398	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
399	```
400	
401	The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob
402	`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for
403	the pattern `title`. If you ran
404	
405	```
406	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
407	```
408	
409	Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not
410	part of ripgrep's built-in types.
411	
412	It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the
413	current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a
414	persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command,
415	then you should either create a shell alias:
416	
417	```
418	alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
419	```
420	
421	or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.
422	([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.)
423	
424	#### The special `all` file type
425	
426	A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks
427	for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,
428	including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent
429	to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...`
430	stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`.
431	
432	As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory,
433	`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`.
434	Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in
435	`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched
436	by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the
437	other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not
438	`my-shell-library.bash`.

{"file_path":"<path>","content":"# Filtering by file type

You search text for a living, so you already write the same globs over and over.
When you only want Rust files, you reach for `-g '*.rs'`. When you want C, you
reach for `-g '*.{c,h}'`, because you have to remember headers too. A file type
is just a name for one or more of those globs, so you write the name instead of
the pattern. ripgrep ships with a set of predefined types for well-known
formats, and you can add your own.

## `-t/--type`: search only one type

Point ripgrep at a type and it searches only files that match that type's
globs:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The short form takes its value with no space. A type is a name assigned to one
or more globs, so a single name can stand in for a broad set of extensions. The
`c` type covers both source and headers:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

Pass `-t` more than once and the types add up. `rg -trust -tmarkdown` searches
files matching either type.

Note that `--type` has lower precedence than the `-g/--glob` flag and than any
rules found in ignore files. A type selection restricts what you search; it does
not override a `.gitignore` entry or an explicit glob.

There is one special value. `--type all` behaves as if you had passed `--type`
for every type ripgrep knows, including any you added on the command line. The
effect is a whitelist: ripgrep searches only files it recognizes and skips
everything else.

## `-T/--type-not`: exclude a type

Just as you can write a blacklist glob, you can blacklist a type:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

So `-t` means "include files of this type" and `-T` means "exclude files of
this type." Both flags stack, and you can mix them in one command
(`rg -Trust -ttoml -Tjson`).

`--type-not all` is the mirror of `--type all`: it excludes every recognized
type, leaving only files ripgrep does not recognize. That distinction turns on
file names, so it's worth a concrete case. Suppose you have `my-shell-script`
(no extension) and `my-shell-library.bash`. Both `rg --type sh` and
`rg --type all` search only `my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh` type's
globs don't match a name without an extension. `rg --type-not all` does the
reverse: it searches `my-shell-script` and skips the `.bash` file.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

To see the types you can use, and the globs behind each one, run:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each type prints on its own line, then a `:`, then a comma-delimited list of its
globs. Pipe the output back through ripgrep to find one:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

The list reflects any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags on the same command,
so it's also how you check that a type you defined came out the way you meant.

## `--type-add`: define your own

When a set of globs is yours and not one of the built-ins, name it. Say you
often search "web" files, meaning JavaScript, HTML, and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

Each `--type-add` adds one glob, so you can pass the flag several times. A brace
pattern collapses that to one:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

That defines the type `web`, applies it with `-tweb`, and searches for `title`.
The spec is `name:glob`, and type names may contain only Unicode letters or
numbers, no punctuation.

You can also build a type out of other types with the `include` directive. It
takes one or more existing type names, separated by commas, and pulls their
globs in:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
```

Add more globs to `src` afterward with another `--type-add 'src:*.foo'`. To
start a type over rather than extend it, clear it first with `--type-clear
<name>`, then add.

Note that `--type-add` applies only to the command you run it on. It does not
save anything; the next `rg` invocation won't know about `web`. To make a type
permanent, put it where every invocation sees it. A shell alias works:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

Or add the line to your ripgrep configuration file, which is the tidier home for
settings you always want:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

Either way, `--type-list` will then show `web` alongside the built-in types
every time.
"}

Done. Written to `DOCUMENT.md` (743 words of prose, zero em dashes).

Every claim is grounded in the tree:

- **`-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`** — flag docs, short/long forms, and the `-trust`/`-Trust` no-space parsing from `crates/core/flags/defs.rs`; the union-of-selections and whitelist behaviour from `matched()` in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`; the "lower precedence than `--glob` and ignore rules" note verbatim from the `--type` doc.
- **`all`** — the whitelist/blacklist semantics from both flag docs, and the `my-shell-script` / `.bash` extensionless example straight from `GUIDE.md`.
- **`--type-list`** — the one-line-per-type `name: glob, glob` format and its reflection of `--type-add`/`--type-clear`, with the real `make:` output from the guide.
- **`--type-add`** — one-glob-per-flag, the `name:glob` spec, letters/numbers-only names, the `include:cpp,py,md` directive, the `--type-clear` companion, and the "not persisted → alias or config file" workaround.

I followed ripgrep's own voice: lowercase "ripgrep", `rg` in shell lines, "flag", short second-person sentences, the literal answer first, and demonstrations rather than superlatives. Nothing else was written to disk.
